subject: Testing how "unnormal" some data might be.

messages.author: 18a7edc32c6cb44d
messages.subject: Testing how "unnormal" some data might be.
parts:
Hello Group,

I've been searching the web for an answer to this question but have
yet to find one.

What I am currently doing.

The following produces a density plot of the numeric data and overlays
a normal curve. The normal curve is derived from the numeric data's
mean, standard deviation, min and max values. This creates a graph
that is easy to visually evaluate how skewed or un-normal the density
of the data being analyzed is.

object1 <- c(1, 1, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 7, 7, 7, 7,7,7, 8, 9, 9, 10)
#not real data, the real set is 500+ numbers
object1.d <- density(object1)
plot(object1.d)
plot(function(x)dnorm(x,mean=mean(object1),sd=sd(object1)), max
(object1.d$x),min(object1.d$x), add=TRUE, lty=1,lwd=3)

where object1 is a numeric variable.

What I'm trying to do.

I would like a more robust / valid method with which to determine how
close to normal my data's density plot is. Essentially I would like to
compare the generated value to the actual value and determine if the
difference between the two is significant or past some thresh hold.
Another approach would be just to see how normal my data is, but I am
unsure of how to do that as well. This was the best approach I could
come up with at the moment.

What I tried.

temp <- function(x)dnorm(x,mean=mean(object1),sd=sd(object1))
both <- c(temp , object1.d)
cor(both$x, both$y)
#[1] 0.04855779

#I tried rcorr in the Hmisc package so I could get significance
however, I got this error
rcorr(both, type="pearson")
#Error in storage.mode(x) <- if (.R.) "double" else "single" :
#(list) object cannot be coerced to type 'double'

#so I tried to solve it like this

both <- both[c(2,3)] #the only columns I need
rcorr(both, type="pearson")
#Error in storage.mode(x) <- if (.R.) "double" else "single" :
#(list) object cannot be coerced to type 'double'

#so I checked
class(both$x)
#[1] "numeric"
class(both$y)
#[1] "numeric"

confused!?

Of course I don't know if this is the right approach to comparing the
two curves. I would appreciate suggestions on what type of analysis I
could/should do and maybe a suggestion on how to do it.

Thanks everyone!

Ross Hendrickson

Hey all,

I thought I would share what I've found and get some feedback. After talking to another friend I decided on the following method that calculates the difference between the expected value and the observed value, squares the result, and then averages the resulting sum of squares over all observations. While not perfect the resulting number does allow me to compare the relative normality between different observed populations. I then use the mean of the observations to determine how close to ideal (0.5 in this case) the model would be. The results are very much in line with what I expected to find after visually comparing Q-Q plots. I am also checking for normality using Stefan's suggested Shapiro-Wilk test just to make sure (thought not in the following code).

Thanks for everyone's help,

Ross

testF <- function(var1)
{
    #Start at 1.00 as "best" Average Square
    best <- 1;
    bestLevel <- 0;
    values <- unique(var1$syllable_count)
   
    #Iterate over all syllable_counts
    for(i in values)
    {
        #Subset out the current syllable count we are looking at
        temp <- subset(var1, syllable_count == i);
        current <- i;
        temp.qq <- qqnorm(temp$perc)$x;
        qqline(temp$perc);
       
        sum <- 0;
        length <- c(1:length(temp$perc))
        total <- 0
        #Iterates over all the values at a given syllable_count
        for(x in length)
        {
            #Difference between expected and actual squared
            step <- (abs(temp$perc[x])-abs(temp.qq[x]))^2;
            #Sum of Squares
            sum <- sum + step
            out <- step
            total <- total + 1;
        }
       
        #Sum of Squares averaged over the number of observations
        ssum <- sum  / max(length);
       
        mean <- mean(temp$perc);
        mean <- paste("Mean:", mean, sep=" ");
        A2 <- paste("A2:", ssum, sep=" ");
        out <- paste(r2, mean, sep=" ");
        out <- paste(current, out, sep=" ");
        out <- paste("Level", out, sep=" ");
        print(out);
       
        #Compare the recently calculated average square to the lowest previously found
        compare <- ssum;
        if(compare < best)
        {
            best <- compare;
            bestLevel <- i;
        }
        #cor <- cor(temp$perc, temp.qq);
       
    }

    output <- paste("Best Level :", bestLevel, sep=" ");
    output <- paste(output, best, sep=" ");
    print(output);
    #Plot the QQ-plot of the lowest average square found
    temp <- subset(var1, syllable_count == bestLevel);
    qqnorm(temp$perc);
    qqline(temp$perc);

}
